input: Pitch a mentorship program idea to HR

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The program's size, structure, and who it covers (e.g., all employees vs. a specific department, formal vs. informal matching) completely shapes what needs to be pitched and how complex the proposal is.
Knowing who the program is designed for (e.g., new hires, mid-level employees, specific roles) determines the framing, benefits, and talking points of the pitch.
Whether the pitch is a casual conversation, a scheduled meeting, or a formal presentation changes the format and level of preparation needed.
A timeline deadline for when the pitch must happen drives how much preparation time is available and how polished the materials need to be.
The tone and style of the pitch (data-driven vs. story-led, brief overview vs. detailed plan) should align with what typically resonates with this HR team.
The deliverable format — a slide deck, a one-pager, a verbal pitch, an email — determines what actually needs to be created.
Understanding what a successful outcome looks like (e.g., getting a follow-up meeting, full approval, a pilot program greenlit) focuses the pitch on the right call to action.

gold.taskTitle: Pitch a Mentorship Program Idea to HR
gold.taskDescription: Prepare and deliver a compelling pitch to the HR department proposing a new mentorship program within the organization.

questions.title: Which employees is this program designed to serve?
questions.description: Identify the target participants of the mentorship program — e.g., new hires, junior staff, a specific department, or the whole company.

questions.title: What structure does the program follow?
questions.description: Define what the mentorship program actually includes — e.g., one-on-one pairings, group cohorts, cross-departmental matching, a set duration, or recurring sessions.

questions.title: What format will the pitch itself take?
questions.description: Clarify whether this is a formal presentation, a casual conversation, a written proposal, or something else entirely.

questions.title: What deliverable do you need to prepare?
questions.description: Determine the concrete output required — e.g., a slide deck, a one-page brief, a structured email, or just talking points.

questions.title: When does this pitch need to happen?
questions.description: Establish the deadline or scheduled date for the pitch so preparation can be scoped and prioritized accordingly.

questions.title: What tone tends to persuade your HR team?
questions.description: Understand whether the pitch should lean on data and ROI, personal stories and culture, a detailed implementation plan, or a high-level vision.

questions.title: What outcome would make this pitch a success?
questions.description: Define the ideal result — e.g., immediate program approval, a follow-up meeting, a pilot greenlit, or budget allocated.
